title: Success of an Agent-Assisted System that Reduces Email Overload
research_question: Does combining automatic email task extraction with learned task-ordering advice improve novice performance under simulated email overload, and how do users respond to agent errors and critical-task recommendations?
methodology: RADAR was evaluated in a between-subjects conference-planning simulation with three conditions: no learned assistance (None), task-centric email assistance without ordering advice (TC), and task-centric assistance plus Multi-task Coordination Assistant ordering advice (TCO). There were 23, 28, and 28 usable participants respectively, and each participant completed a two-hour test after training. The test inbox contained 123 emails, including 83 emails containing 153 task instances and 40 distracter emails; the classifier operated on 102 task-type labels. Evaluation combined an externally designed objective task-performance score, logged task outcomes and classifier errors, critical-task behavior, and post-test ratings.

key_findings.finding: Participants receiving both task extraction and ordering assistance achieved a mean overall score of 0.754 versus 0.706 with task-centric assistance alone and 0.550 with no learned assistance; the condition effect was significant and the paper summarizes the TCO-versus-None improvement as 37%.
The email classifier was deliberately tuned toward precision and achieved precision 0.887 and recall 0.461, correctly identifying 47 of 102 task labels while producing six false positives.
key_findings.section: Email Classification and the Task-Centric Action List

key_findings.finding: TCO users incorrectly completed an average of 2.6 false-positive or true-negative tasks, compared with 10.3 incorrectly completed tasks in the no-assistance condition, which the authors describe as up to a fourfold reduction in mistakes.
key_findings.section: Email Classification and the Task-Centric Action List

key_findings.finding: TCO participants completed fewer total and fewer non-critical tasks than TC participants but achieved higher overall scores, consistent with the ordering agent steering limited effort toward higher-value obligations and away from overflow work.
key_findings.section: Effects of the MCA's Task Strategy Recommendations

key_findings.finding: The Action List explicitly represented incomplete, overflow, completed, and deleted tasks and allowed users to add missed tasks or delete false positives, providing within-session work-state and correction mechanisms.
Participants complied with 97 of 112 issued critical-task warnings overall, although compliance differed substantially by warning type and users varied widely in how much agent advice they followed.
key_findings.section: Effects of the MCA's Task Strategy Recommendations

key_findings.finding: The authors state that a real deployment could use online learning to continuously adapt to users' choices, but the reported experiment used models learned beforehand from expert demonstrations and did not empirically evaluate preference drift or online personalization.

limitations: The study used a simulated two-hour conference-planning task rather than longitudinal everyday workplace use.
Participants were novices recruited from universities and the general population rather than established teams managing their own ongoing work.
The evaluated task-ordering policy was learned from experts before the study; proposed continuous online adaptation was not tested.
The classifier favored precision at the cost of low recall, leaving many task labels undetected.
Although the interface tracked incomplete, overflow, completed, and deleted tasks, the experiment did not evaluate repeated briefing cycles or explicit superseded-state transitions.
The scenario contained only one briefing-request email, and briefing quality was one component of the final score rather than a repeatedly generated cross-thread briefing.
The study did not measure repetition of already-reported work items across briefings.
No-shows, dropouts, poor-faith participation, software crashes, and configuration problems caused unequal usable sample sizes across conditions.
raw_claims: RADAR converts task-bearing email into a task-centric Action List.
The MCA learns task-performance strategies from demonstrations by expert users.
The evaluated study compared None, TC, and TCO assistance conditions.
The usable samples were 23 participants in None and 28 participants in each assisted condition.
The test inbox contained 123 emails, including 40 unrelated distracter emails.
The classifier found 47 of 102 task labels and produced six false positives.
TCO achieved the highest mean objective evaluation score of the three conditions.
TCO participants completed fewer non-critical tasks than TC participants while scoring better overall.
The interface separated incomplete, overflow, completed, and deleted tasks.
Users could correct classifier false positives and false negatives through the interface.
The MCA identified five critical task types, including sending a briefing.
The paper proposes continuous online adaptation for real deployment but does not test it in the reported experiment.
